title: The Memory Palace of Stone and Light
subtitle: A scroll-driven journey through architecture, sculpture, and the human wish to outlast time.

chapters.title: The First Wall
chapters.text: Before cities, before columns, before kings carved their names into stone, people entered caves and covered darkness with animals, motion, and memory. The wall became a stage, and the image became a way to keep a world alive after the hunt had passed.
chapters.focus: painted bison, mineral pigment, cave wall

chapters.title: The Measured Temple
chapters.text: Classical architecture turned belief into proportion. The Parthenon did not simply stand on the Acropolis; it corrected the eye with subtle curves, slight tilts, and sculpted rhythm, making stone feel almost alive.

chapters.title: The Hole in the Sky
chapters.text: The Pantheon gathers the world beneath a perfect dome and opens it with an oculus. Sunlight enters like a moving hand, crossing stone by the hour and reminding every visitor that architecture can measure time without a clock.

chapters.title: The Floating Dome
chapters.text: Hagia Sophia made mass feel weightless. Its dome seems to hover on light, gold, and geometry, turning engineering into awe. For centuries it taught builders that structure could become atmosphere.

chapters.title: The Body Before Action
chapters.text: Michelangelo’s David is not shown in victory. He is shown in the instant before decision: marble tightened into attention, hand enlarged by purpose, gaze fixed on a future still invisible to us.

chapters.title: Symmetry and Grief
chapters.text: The Taj Mahal transforms mourning into balance. Marble, garden, water, calligraphy, and reflected sky form an architecture of devotion where grief is given proportion and light.

chapters.title: The Workshop Window
chapters.text: The Bauhaus replaced ornament with systems, workshops, and clarity. Glass, steel, typography, and furniture became part of one design language: useful, repeatable, and modern enough to remake daily life.

chapters.title: The House Over the Stream
chapters.text: Fallingwater does not sit beside nature; it negotiates with it. Concrete planes reach over running water, stone rises from the site, and the home becomes a bridge between shelter and landscape.
